body: Size every position from the stop: shares = (account × risk%) ÷ (entry − stop). Keep risk per trade at 0.25-1% (2% hard ceiling), total open risk ("portfolio heat") ≤ ~6-10%, cut losses fast (7-8% max per O'Neil; 3-5% typical for VCP/Qullamaggie), and only add to winners. Positive expectancy with small, uniform R is what lets low-win-rate breakout systems (25-50% win rate) survive.

**Verified price block**
- Screener.in: **₹410**, stamped 19 Nov 2026 3:32 pm. Mcap ₹5,355 cr.
- Bajaj Finserv: ₹414.65 (16 Nov, 3:30 pm). Ventura: NSE ₹415.00 / BSE ₹412.80 (16 Nov). ICICI Direct: ₹423.90 (17 Nov, 9:18 am; labelled a close, but the timing makes that doubtful).
- **Price used: ~₹410.** The sources sit within 3% of each other, which fits normal day-to-day moves.
- Re-derived P/E: ₹5,355 cr / TTM PAT ₹251 cr = **21.3×**, which matches the 21.4× shown on screener.
- 52-week range ~₹243–692. The stock rallied about 150% in H1 2026, then fell ~41% from its high. It dropped 11% on Q1 results (Jul) and 8–10% on Q2 results (15 Oct), despite PAT growth of 66–80% in both quarters.

**Financials (consolidated, ₹cr)**

| FY | Sales | OPM | PAT | ROCE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY22 | 880 | 20% | 170 | 38% |
| FY23 | 961 | 15% | 139 | 26% |
| FY24 | 984 | 16% | 155 | 21% |
| FY25 | 965 | 13% | 125 | 23% |
| FY26 | 1,165 | 19% | 190 | 19% |
| TTM | 1,307 | 23% | 251 | 30% (latest) |

| Qtr | Mar-25 | Jun-25 | Sep-25 | Dec-25 | Mar-26 | Jun-26 | Sep-26 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sales | 250 | 273 | 265 | 306 | 327 | 342 | 333 |
| OPM | 13% | 15% | 18% | 18% | 23% | 24% | 25% |
| PAT | 31 | 38 | 42 | 46 | 64 | 71 | 70 |

There is no loss quarter, and the margin rise holds across 7 consecutive quarters rather than resting on one spike. Other income is steady at ₹5–9 cr a quarter and the tax rate at 17–19%, so the PAT jump is operating, not driven by other income.

**Balance sheet and holders.** Borrowings ₹4–16 cr over FY23–Sep-26 (debt-free). Debtor days rose from 8 (FY22) to 24–27 (FY25–26). That needs watching, but it is still low.

Shareholding, Dec-24 → Sep-26:
- Promoter: 40.95% → 42.97%. The step came from the Sep 2025 buyback (₹290/sh, ₹187 cr, promoters did not tender). It was the second buyback at ₹290 in two years.
- FII: 10.5% → **16.4%**, rising, with a step-up in Mar-26.
- DII: 20.2% → 14.9%, falling.

Pledge: none was flagged on screener and none came up in searches. The promoter family cleared a pledge in 2019 by selling ~22%. That history, and the group's Bajaj Hindusthan links, are a governance memory to keep in mind. **I could not confirm the current pledge figure from an NSE filing.**

**Structural story and named cause.** The margin went from 13% to 25%, which is a return toward the company's FY18–19 level of ~30%. Q2 FY27 sales were +25% and EBITDA +71% to ₹83.3 cr, at a 25.0% margin vs 18.6% (JM Financial). The company cites three drivers:
1. Double-digit **unit volume** growth in Almond Drops (10%+), with domestic Almond Drops revenue up >30% in H1.
2. Coconut-portfolio volumes ahead of value, because coconut prices deflated.
3. Price-point packs growing faster than the rest of the portfolio, plus distribution expansion.

- What is available: buying quality franchises during pessimism (Titan in 2001-02, HDFC Bank, D-Mart's cost model as a thesis), holding for decades, and sizing up with conviction.

`person:samir-arora` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: india, process, growth, risk-management

CIO of Alliance Capital's Indian MF business 1993-Aug 2003 (funds won 15+ awards); founded Helios Capital (Singapore) in 2005; Helios MF in India launched 2023-24 (its flexi-cap fund has posted strong early returns per Value Research). A Morningstar/PMS-AIF profile claims ~25% a year (219x) since 1996 vs ~12.2% (16x) for the Indian market in INR - combining Alliance and Helios records (single-source, unaudited). His 2003 departure from Alliance followed a SEBI order that was later overturned on appeal (details not re-verified here). Process edge: (1) an 'avoid list' - he excludes whole sectors with poor long-run shareholder returns or governance (PSUs, many commodities, utilities, real estate) to cut error rates; (2) sell losers early rather than average down; (3) diversified 30-40 stock portfolios in growth sectors (private financials, consumer, tech); (4) he argues fewer than 5% of stocks are worth holding long term, so 'buy and hold' alone is not enough. Mistakes: the avoid list made Helios miss the 2021-24 PSU/defence/railway rally (characterisation); he cut equity sharply in early 2020 on COVID (reported; unverified) and had to re-enter. Copyable: write your own avoid list (sectors with chronic capital destruction), set a sell rule for thesis-broken losers, and accept missing some rallies as the price of fewer blow-ups.

`strategy:greenblatt-special-situations` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: global, india, process, special-situations, value

Two separate methods. (A) Special situations (You Can Be a Stock Market Genius): spin-offs (parent holders sell the unwanted child regardless of price; insiders often get equity incentives in the new entity), restructurings, merger securities, rights offerings, recapitalisations and LEAPS. Edge comes from non-economic selling and small size. Indian analogues: demergers (e.g., recent conglomerate splits), open offers and buyback arbitrage, rights issues priced at deep discounts. (B) Magic Formula (2005): rank stocks by return on capital = EBIT / (net working capital + net fixed assets) and earnings yield = EBIT / enterprise value, sum ranks, buy top 20-30, hold one year, repeat; exclude financials/utilities. Backtest 1988-2004: ~30.8%/yr vs ~12.4% for the S&P 500; live results were much weaker, and multi-year underperformance led most users to abandon it - Greenblatt's own point is that it works because it is hard to stick with. Use as an idea generator plus a quality/governance check in India, where cheap high-ROC stocks often include cyclicals at peak margins and promoter-governance risks.
